Sacramento investment Opportunities

Sacramento-area listings, screened as buy-and-hold or short-term-rental candidates.       Which ZIP code should you even be looking in?

      The table on the Investment Ledger tab scores individual comps — this tab steps back a level and scores the areas those comps come from, so the daily search and manual address checks can be pointed at the right ZIP codes in the first place. Each area is scored 0–100 across the same six weighted factors regardless of state: schools, crime & safety, affordability, ADU feasibility, short-term-rental market & regulatory fit, and commute — split below into California, Texas, and Arizona tabs. California's eleven Sacramento-metro areas were built from Tony's own ZIP-ranking research plus independent verification — CrimeGrade.org crime data (the shared thread didn't cover crime at all), live Niche.com grades, and four specific Sacramento/Roseville/Davis/El Dorado Hills policy questions resolved directly against ordinance text. Arizona's 26 Phoenix-metro areas (school score above 6, median price at or below $400K) were researched the same way — Niche.com schools, CrimeGrade.org crime, Redfin pricing, and jurisdiction-level ADU/STR regulatory research covering Arizona's statewide ADU preemption (HB 2720/2928) and STR preemption (A.R.S. §9-500.39) laws. Texas's 8 Austin-metro areas were researched the same way, starting from a 42-ZIP Austin + Austin-metro universe (Austin proper plus Cedar Park, Leander, Round Rock, Georgetown, Buda, Kyle, and Dripping Springs) narrowed by two hard filters — every ZIP confirmed west of Interstate 35, and the same school-score-above-6/price-at-or-below-$400K bar used for Arizona — which is a far more restrictive combination here than it was for Phoenix, since Austin-metro's generally higher price point and the I-35 exclusion (which removes the metro's traditionally more affordable east-side ZIPs) leave only a handful of qualifying areas rather than two dozen. Two more ZIPs were added afterward at Tony's explicit request as deliberate price-cap overrides, each clearing the I-35 and school-score bars but missing the $400K price cap: 78729 (Anderson Mill, by about $49K) and 78745 (South Austin, by about $31K) — both scored and flagged rather than silently folded in as if they had cleared the cap on their own.

      Scoring rubric — 100 points
      Open questions & things to double-check before acting on these scores
      1. Sacramento's ADU-short-term-rental cap is genuinely in flux. The city currently caps STR nights on ADU/accessory structures at 90/year city-wide, and a City Council vote on loosening that cap has been publicly discussed but not finalized as of this research — treat any of the five Sacramento-city ZIPs' STR-fit score as a snapshot, not a guarantee, and re-check the city's short-term-rental ordinance page before underwriting an ADU-STR strategy there.
      2. Folsom's (95630) property-crime grade is a real outlier against the city's general reputation as one of the safer Sacramento suburbs — D- on CrimeGrade's property-crime measure, the single worst property-crime rate of all 11 areas. Worth confirming directly with Folsom PD before fully trusting it; it's possible this reflects a data quirk (a small number of ZIP-level incidents skewing the per-1,000 rate) rather than a genuine safety problem.
      3. Davis (95618) has a genuine STR-legality gap — unlike every other area on this page, Davis's municipal code does not clearly permit whole-home short-term rentals in residential zones, and no definitive city guidance resolving this was found. Its STR-fit score reflects that uncertainty as a real regulatory risk, not just a soft "check locally" caveat.
      4. Two price figures carry sourcing discrepancies. 95747 (Roseville-west) and 95762 (El Dorado Hills) each had more than one home-price source with a meaningfully different number; the price used here is flagged in that area's card with the specific range seen.
      5. 95762's crime data is a city-level proxy, not ZIP-specific — no CrimeGrade page exists for that exact ZIP, so El Dorado Hills' city-level violent/property crime grades were used as the closest available substitute.
      6. This is a screening rubric built from public data, not a substitute for walking these neighborhoods, talking to a local agent, or pulling a full CrimeGrade/Niche report for your final short list.

        Where are prices headed next — USA, California, Arizona, Texas?

        A quarterly house-price forecasting pipeline covering the national market and all three states on this dashboard, trained on FHFA’s all-transactions House Price Index (1975–2026) plus a stack of macro inputs from FRED — mortgage rates, unemployment, inflation, population, construction permits/starts, the S&P 500, mortgage delinquency, and gasoline prices. Ten candidate models were backtested per market and per forecast horizon using an annual expanding-window walk-forward scheme (fit once a year, test the following year, never look ahead); the lowest-error model from a 1990–2013 selection window is frozen and then graded strictly out-of-sample from 2014 onward. That backtested, out-of-sample-graded model is what produces the three-quarter forecast below.

        Built from a research pipeline Tony ran and shared (full data, code, and a 69-page backtest export reviewed line by line below) — independently reviewed here, cross-checked against outside forecasting literature, and extended with an honest look at where the current approach could be improved. Nothing on this tab is a recommendation to buy, sell, or time a purchase around a quarterly house-price index.

        Latest FHFA-published quarter: 2026 Q2. The models below estimate the three quarters after it — Q3 2026 (a nowcast of an unpublished quarter), Q4 2026, and Q1 2027 — each compounded onto the last published index to build a path. The shaded band on every chart is an empirical 80% interval built from that model’s own historical walk-forward errors, not a statistical guarantee, and (per the coverage figures further down this tab) it doesn’t always land exactly on 80% in practice.

        What’s actually driving the Q1 2027 forecast, market by market

        Permutation importance for each market’s Q1-2027 model: how much worse that model’s error gets when a factor group is shuffled. A longer bar to the right means the model is leaning on that factor group for real; a bar to the left (negative) means shuffling it didn’t hurt — the model isn’t using it much at this horizon.

        Which macro factors move house prices most — ranked across all 4 markets

        Averaging each factor group's permutation importance across all 4 markets and all 3 forecast horizons (12 backtested champion-model runs total) gives one overall ranking, rather than reading four separate per-market bar charts. The gap between factors matters as much as the order: a property's own price history and new-construction supply dominate every one of these backtests, while most individual macro series add only marginal measured lift once those two are already in the model.

        Methodology, in the pipeline’s own terms

        Annual expanding-window backtest — how training and testing actually worked

        Price history runs back to 1975; FHFA has no comparable state-level panel for 1970–1974, so none was invented. Most macro features start in 1977. For each origin year from 1990 onward, the model fits once on all labels through the prior calendar year, then forecasts that year’s quarters with parameters held fixed — only after the year completes does it add those observations and refit for the next year. That’s annual expanding-window retraining, not a random train/test split, and it means no future quarter ever leaks into an earlier fold. Horizon 0/1/2 target the unpublished origin quarter, the one after it, and the one after that, as quarterly log price changes; the Q1 2027 figure on this tab is a horizon-2 forecast made from a Q3 2026 origin. Model choice (the champion column above) is frozen using validation performance through 2013 only, then everything from 2014 onward — including every number in the scorecard and regime tables above — is strictly out-of-sample. Imputers and scalers are refit separately inside each training fold; no full-sample scaling or interpolation is used anywhere. The production forecast on this tab is one final refit of the already-selected specification on every quarter published through Q2 2026, using Q3 2026 macro inputs available as of the research date — that final refit is not what generated the backtest numbers above.

        Known limitations — read before trusting a single forecast quarter
        • Not a crash detector. High direction-accuracy numbers above are mostly rising-price quarters. The selected horizon-2 models caught only 0 of 1 declining U.S. quarters, 1 of 7 in California, 0 of 4 in Arizona, and 0 of 2 in Texas during the 2014-onward evaluation.
        • The 2007–2012 window isn’t an untouched crisis holdout. Those years were part of model selection, not a clean out-of-sample stress test — treat that regime row as informative, not as proof the model would catch the next downturn.
        • Interval coverage isn’t always 80%. A stricter check — intervals calibrated on pre-2014 data only, evaluated 2014-onward — shows coverage varying by market and horizon; Texas runs weaker than the nominal 80% target (see the scorecard above).
        • Some real drivers aren’t in the data at all. Fifty years of consistent quarterly series don’t exist for local MLS inventory, insurance cost/availability, investor flows, underwriting standards, household formation, local migration, or equity-compensation income — the macro proxies used here don’t fully substitute for those.
        • Backtests use revised history, not real-time vintages. FHFA and FRED series were pulled as currently published, not as they stood on each historical forecast date — this can make the backtest look slightly better than live forecasting would have been.
        • Permutation importance isn’t causal. Correlated macro features and regime shifts mean a factor’s importance score reflects what the model leaned on in its fitting window, not a proven economic cause-and-effect.

        Independent review: is there a better model, or a better train/test window?

        This part is separate from reviewing Tony’s pipeline above — outside literature was pulled specifically to stress-test the model choice and the expanding-window design, per the request to look for something better.

        Confirms the pipelineAnnual expanding-window walk-forward is the right default here

        Walk-forward validation — fit, forecast forward, then roll the window ahead — is described as the time-series field’s standard evaluation method, specifically because it mirrors how a model would actually be used in production and avoids the look-ahead bias a random train/test split would introduce (Brownlee, “How To Backtest Machine Learning Models for Time Series Forecasting,” MachineLearningMastery). A direct comparison of expanding vs. rolling windows adds the nuance that an expanding window suits a series where older history still carries signal and needs no window-size hyperparameter to tune, at the cost of reacting more slowly after a structural break (“Rolling vs. Expanding Window Cross-Validation,” MetricGate). A 50-year housing-price panel with a handful of distinct regimes (the 1980s run-up, the 2008 crash, the 2021–22 boom) is a reasonable fit for the expanding choice Tony’s pipeline already makes.

        Confirms the pipelineNo single model family dominates — which is exactly why a champion is picked per market and horizon

        A 2023 comparison of machine-learning and classical statistical forecasting methods found that tree-based ML models (random forest, especially on differenced inputs) performed best in some regimes, while classical models held up just as well or better in others — the authors’ conclusion was explicitly that no one approach wins universally (arXiv:2303.07139). That matches what the candidate-model grid above actually shows: Ridge-blend models win most often, but Random Forest takes California’s longer horizons and both of Texas’s near-term horizons. The pipeline’s per-market, per-horizon selection is the right response to that finding, not a shortcut around it.

        Possible improvementA classical/ML hybrid is a concrete, untested 11th candidate

        A study forecasting a national housing price index found that a hybrid ARIMA + Random Forest model outperformed either model run alone, reasoning that ARIMA captures the linear trend/seasonality while the random forest mops up the nonlinear residual pattern ARIMA misses (“Forecasting of Turkish Housing Price Index: ARIMA, Random Forest, ARIMA-Random Forest”). The current 10-candidate field has a price-history ridge model and a Ridge/macro blend that play a similar role, but no explicit ARIMA-plus-tree-ensemble hybrid. Worth adding as an 11th candidate on the next retrain — cheap to test given the pipeline already has the walk-forward harness built.

        Possible improvementThe 2020–2022 weak spot may be the expanding window’s own blind spot

        The regime table above shows RMSE roughly doubling to tripling in every market during the 2020–2022 stretch — the Fed’s rate-shock period — compared to the calm 2014–2019 years. That lines up with the literature’s stated weakness of expanding windows: because old regimes keep diluting the fit, an expanding window reacts more slowly right after a structural break, whereas a rolling window drops stale history and adapts faster at the cost of noisier estimates (same MetricGate comparison above). A concrete next test: run the same 10 candidates with a rolling 15–20-year training window instead of an expanding one, grid-searching the window length against post-2020 RMSE specifically, and see whether it closes any of that rate-shock gap without hurting accuracy in the calm years.

        Caveat, not a flawTreat the shaded band as a rough guide, not a guarantee

        The pipeline’s own stricter coverage check (intervals calibrated only on pre-2014 errors, checked against 2014-onward outcomes) already flags that real coverage runs below the nominal 80% in some market/horizon pairs — Texas most noticeably. Independent research didn’t surface a reason to doubt that finding; if anything, empirically-calibrated intervals on a 50-year series with regime shifts almost always drift from their nominal target over time, so re-checking coverage after each future quarterly refresh is worth building into the pipeline’s own validation step.

        Does 2026 rhyme with the 1970s–80s energy-shock years?

        Gasoline jumped from $3.26/gal in 2025 to $3.97/gal in 2026 on this tab's own data above — a ~22% one-year move — while inflation ticked back up to 3.1% and the 30-year mortgage rate is still stuck near 6.5%. That combination (an energy-price spike landing on top of already-elevated inflation) is the same basic shape as the 1973 oil embargo and 1979 energy crisis, and it's why financial commentary this year has reached for 1970s/"stagflation" comparisons. Worth stress-testing with real numbers rather than just the vibe: did house prices and gasoline prices actually move together back then?

        Two honesty notes before the chart. First, scope: the user asked for 1970–1989, but neither series used elsewhere on this tab reaches back that far — the gasoline $/gal series starts 1976, and the FHFA house-price index starts 1975. So this chart swaps in two different, equally real federal series chosen specifically because they run without a gap across the full 1970–1989 window: BLS's CPI index for motor fuel (continuous monthly since 1935) for gasoline, and the Census Bureau/HUD median sales price of new houses sold (continuous quarterly since 1963) for house prices — a narrower "new homes only" measure, not the broader FHFA repeat-sales index used on the rest of this tab. Second, units: a price index and a dollar figure can't honestly share one axis unscaled, so both lines below are indexed to 1970 = 100 — pure rescaling, which does not change the correlation reported underneath.

        On price levelsr = 0.77 — strong, but mostly a shared trend

        Pearson correlation on the 20 real annual values (not the indexed ones — indexing doesn't change this number) is r ≈ 0.77 (R² ≈ 0.59) over 1970–1989. That's a strong positive correlation, but both series were rising almost every year of this period — gasoline through 1970s inflation and two oil shocks, house prices through ordinary demand growth plus the same inflation. Two series that both trend upward for 20 years will correlate strongly on level alone even if their year-to-year moves aren't actually linked — so this number mostly confirms "both went up a lot in the 1970s," which is already visible in the chart.

        On year-over-year changer ≈ 0.08 — essentially no short-term co-movement

        Correlating the two series' year-over-year % changes instead (which cancels out the shared trend and asks "did a bigger gas-price jump in a given year coincide with a bigger house-price jump that same year?") gives r ≈ 0.08 — close to zero. The 1979–1981 gasoline spike, for example, didn't produce a matching spike in house-price growth; house prices kept rising at a fairly steady pace through the whole period regardless of what gasoline did year to year. Read together, the two numbers say: gasoline and house prices shared the same inflationary decade, but gasoline-price shocks specifically don't look like a reliable short-term driver of house-price moves in this data.
